opus-5.5.text:
I think it's been one of the clearer examples of how much the underlying model matters for agents. With the earlier versions of Operator, the idea was right, but the reliability wasn't there. It would get partway through a task, click the wrong thing, lose track of what it was doing, or confidently do something you didn't want. And with agents, small error rates compound. If you're ninety percent reliable on each step and a task has twenty steps, you basically never finish. That was the core problem we kept running into.

Moving Operator onto o3 helped because reasoning models are much better at the things agents actually need: planning over multiple steps, noticing when something has gone wrong, backing up and trying another approach, and knowing when to stop and ask the user instead of guessing. That last one matters a lot for safety and trust. You want an agent that pauses before entering your credit card or sending an email on your behalf, not one that barrels ahead.

I don't want to overstate it. It's still early, it still makes mistakes, and there are plenty of tasks where you'd be frustrated with it. But it went from feeling like a cool demo to feeling like something you might actually hand a real chore to. To me that's the signal that this is a trajectory, not a one-off. Each step up in model capability makes agents disproportionately more useful, because you're cutting that compounding error. I expect the next year or two of agents to feel very different from what people have seen so far.

r001.rationale: The response describes earlier Operator versions as unreliable, making wrong clicks, losing track, and compounding errors. It does not clearly identify the specific brittleness of falling apart when an agent encounters a problem it cannot solve.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the switch to o3 was the moment Operator started to feel like the thing we'd been describing rather than a demo of it.

The problems we had with earlier agentic systems weren't really about any single capability. The model could click the right button most of the time. The issue was that "most of the time" compounds badly. If you've got a task that takes forty steps and each step is ninety-eight percent reliable, you end up with something that fails more often than it succeeds, and it fails in ways that are frustrating because the model doesn't notice it's gone off the rails. It would confidently keep going down a bad path, or get stuck in a loop re-reading the same page, or hand back something that looked finished but wasn't.

What o3 brought was mostly better judgment about its own state. It reasons before acting, it's much better at recognizing when something didn't work and backing up, and it's better at knowing when to stop and ask the person rather than guess. That last part matters more than it sounds. A lot of the trust problem with agents is that people are nervous about handing over a browser, and the thing that makes you comfortable is watching the model pause at the right moments, like before a purchase or when a form is ambiguous.

I'd also say we were deliberate about not rushing it. Moving Operator onto a stronger reasoning model only makes sense if the safety work moves with it. A more capable agent that's also more susceptible to prompt injection on a webpage is a worse product, not a better one. So a lot of the effort went into refusals, confirmation behavior, and making sure the thing is harder to manipulate through content it reads along the way.

Is it solved? No. Long-horizon reliability is still the frontier, and there's a gap between what works in a benchmark and what works when someone's actually trying to book a trip on a badly designed airline site. But the trajectory felt right to me. Each generation of model closes more of the gap between what an agent can do in principle and what you'd actually trust it to do unsupervised, and o3 was a real step on that curve.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier systems could fail to recover when something went wrong, continuing down a bad path or getting stuck in a loop. This conveys their brittleness when they hit an obstacle they cannot handle.

astra-6.text:
I’d judge it by whether it makes the whole task more reliable. With an agent, getting the next step right isn’t enough. It has to keep track of what you wanted, recognize when something went wrong, and recover without making the problem worse.

So the question with the switch to o3 is: does better reasoning translate into better performance over that entire sequence? Does it know when to keep going and when to ask you? A system that can do something impressive once is exciting. A system you can consistently delegate work to is useful. That’s the bar I’d use.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should recognize problems and recover, but it does not identify earlier agentic systems as tending to fall apart when they encounter a problem they cannot solve.

sol-6.1.text: I’d judge it by whether it actually addresses those problems in practice. A stronger reasoning model can help, but an agent has to do more than give a good answer—it has to take the right actions, recognize when it’s uncertain, and recover when something goes wrong. So the switch to o3 is promising, but the real test is whether Operator becomes more reliable on tasks people actually need it to do, including knowing when to stop and ask for help.
